jina.snippet:
Dear Shareholders, 

The first quarter was another outstanding quarter for Carvana. 

It was our 6th consecutive quarter of 40% or greater year-over-year unit growth leading to company records in retail units sold, revenue, gross profit, SG&A expense per unit, GAAP Operating Income, and Adjusted EBITDA, again demonstrating the power of our business model. 

At its core, the used car industry is a complex system that enables customers to switch cars with one another. Our goal is to make that system dramatically simpler, more efficient, more scalable, and more customer-centric. We achieve that through vertical integration, reengineering physical processes, and maximizing the use of technology. 

It’s working. 

The simplest proof point is this: for the 9th straight quarter, we were both the fastest growing and most profitable automotive retailer. 

Another expression of this is how quickly we can move cars from one owner to the next.

Carvana’s Q1 2026 print, reported April 29, was the tenth consecutive quarter as the fastest-growing automotive retailer in America and the sixth consecutive quarter of 40%+ year-over-year retail unit growth. Revenue of $6.43 billion grew 52%, beating the $6.08 billion consensus by 7%. Diluted EPS of $1.69 exceeded the $1.43 LSEG estimate by 18%. Retail units of 187,393 set an all-time quarterly record, up 40% YoY. Adjusted EBITDA of $672 million was an all-time record, up 38% YoY. GAAP operating income of $581 million was an all-time record. By every operational metric that matters, Carvana delivered.

And yet the stock sits in an unusual position. Shares closed at approximately $407 on the day of the print (down 0.7% in regular trading), and after-hours moved sideways despite the records. The stock is roughly flat year-to-date despite earnings up 50%+, and is still 14% below its January 2026 peak of $478 even after rallying 35% off the March $300 lows. The market is engaged in a debate that the operating performance keeps trying to settle: are these record numbers sustainable, or is the company hitting a margin ceiling at 1.6% of US used car market share that will limit how much further this can go?
